The record:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: MetricsAbsent on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: No metrics received from io-shop since 2026-11-11T02:35:00Z {A1} - 5m {A2} with no sample, against a scrape interval of 15 {A3} seconds. The series stopped rather than crossing a threshold, so nothing here says whether the shop is well: these minutes have no readings to judge, not readings that look bad.
Alert raised: 2026-11-11T02:40:55Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-11T02:40:58Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule fires as soon as its condition holds. The alert came 3 minutes 25 seconds {beyond_accounted_for} later than the 2 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute the metrics' stopping is measured to. The record does not show what took the rest.
No metrics were collected from 2026-11-11T02:35:00Z {metrics_stopped_at} (the onset, dated to its minute: a change came during that minute) onwards: the metrics had still not resumed by 2026-11-11T02:43:36Z {argus_stopped}. That is 8 minutes 36 seconds {duration} the metrics did not cover, not a stretch the service is known to have spent in trouble.
Log lines read reach into it until 2026-11-11T02:40:00Z {logs_reach_until}: [G46bc], [Gbac1]. They are the service's own account of that stretch: what they report there is what is known of how it was doing, and up to then the service was seen through them. The logs were read up to 2026-11-11T02:40:55Z {log_reading_ended}, when the alert was raised - nothing after that was read.
How the service did over that stretch is said by the document itself, from your answer to logs_show_serving_as_before: say nothing of it anywhere else. Where the chain's first step says nobody using the service saw anything wrong, cite those log lines for it without saying what they show.
Argus held the incident for 2 minutes 40 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-11T02:43:36Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
Error rate: not measured by the metrics - none were collected after the metrics stopped; the log lines that reach into that stretch, [G46bc], [Gbac1], are the service's own account of it, so do not say nothing was measured; what they show is said by the document itself, from your answer to logs_show_serving_as_before.
Customer loss: none so far - the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all; a lower bound, counted with the service not seen back to normal.

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - name them by their labels, but cite none; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1, also C2] Candidates blaming the same move of deploy/values-production.yaml, each reading it as a different kind of failure - different accounts of what it did, not one cause counted twice - each in its own words:
      C1: The deployment at 2026-11-11T02:35:15Z {C1.1} renamed every port to the estate-wide `<protocol>[-<purpose>]` convention. This included the metrics port, which went from `metrics` to `http-metrics`. The scrape still selects the old name, so the metrics stopped at 2026-11-11T02:35:00Z {C1.2}. The shop itself kept serving at its usual error level. [monitoring-configuration-drift, confidence 0.82 {C1.3}, never tried: the only action that would test the candidate undoes a change that was made on purpose]
      C2: The deployment changed a configuration value (the metrics port name) and broke scraping. This is the same change, read as an unintended breakage instead of a deliberate convention. [monitoring-blind-spot, confidence 0.12 {C1.4}, never tried: the only action that would test the candidate undoes a change that was made on purpose]

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault, as main holds it: `deploy/values-production.yaml` names the metrics port `http-metrics` (`metrics.portName: http-metrics`), but `deploy/scrape.yaml`, the ServiceMonitor, still picks its endpoint with `port: metrics`. The comment in scrape.yaml says the ServiceMonitor finds the endpoint by the port's name, and that a name matching no port gives "a target list with nothing in it" rather than an error. So with these two files as they are, Prometheus has nothing to scrape. That fits the metrics stopping while the shop kept serving.
      
      About the deployed revision: c3c36da3c66c07707f227b7e70b26813083061f3 is not in main's history, and I haven't read it. The investigation describes its change as `ports.metrics.portName`, which is a different key path from main's `metrics.portName`. All I can say about c3c36da is what the investigation reports: it renamed the metrics port to `http-metrics` and the scrape still asks for `metrics`. Everything else here describes main.
      
      The fix: in `deploy/scrape.yaml`, change the endpoint's `port: metrics` to `port: http-metrics` so it matches the name in values-production.yaml. That makes the renamed port safe to keep, so it doesn't need rolling back. Nothing under `src/` reads the port name; the comment in values-production.yaml says so too.
      
      The test: the scrape.yaml comment says "Nothing checks that the two agree", so I added `tests/io_shop/test_scrape_config.py` as that check. It reads `portName` from the `metrics:` block of values-production.yaml and every `port:` entry under the ServiceMonitor's `endpoints:`, then asserts they match. It uses plain line reading, because I found no YAML library imported anywhere in the repository. Against main as it stands, it should fail, comparing `metrics` with `http-metrics`. With this change it should pass, and it should catch the next rename that only updates one of the two files. Nothing has run it yet.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'. [F1] was written against main, which does not contain the revision running when the alert fired: merged, its fix changes what runs only once a deploy carries it. [F1] names revision c3c36da3c66c07707f227b7e70b26813083061f3 and [D1] is that revision's own diff - say what it shows rather than ask for it to be checked.

What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired:
  - [S1] deploy/scrape.yaml at c3c36da
      # How the platform's Prometheus collects the shop's metrics.
      #
      # It selects the shop's Service by label, then the endpoint to scrape on that
      # Service by the port's *name* - never its number - so a port can move without
      # anything here being touched.
      #
      # The name here has to be the one `metrics.portName` in values-production.yaml
      # gives the port. Nothing checks that the two agree: a name that matches no port
      # is not an error to the operator, it is a target list with nothing in it.
      apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
      kind: ServiceMonitor
      metadata:
        name: io-shop
        labels:
          release: prometheus
      spec:
        selector:
          matchLabels:
            app: io-shop
        endpoints:
          - port: metrics
            path: /metrics
            interval: 15s {S1.1}
      
  - [S2] deploy/values-production.yaml at c3c36da
      # Deployment configuration for the io-shop account service, production.
      #
      # Rendered into the cluster as a ConfigMap and mounted into the pod, which is
      # why the service reads this file rather than being handed environment
      # variables: the values here are the deployment's, not the code's, and changing
      # one is a change to configuration that ships without the service being rebuilt.
      #
      # Owned by whoever runs the shop. Changes here go out the way any other change
      # goes out - reviewed, merged, and synced by the platform - and land without a
      # single line of io-shop's source being touched.
      
      replicas: 3 {S2.1}
      
      resources:
        memoryLimitMiB: 2048 {S2.2}
      
      # How the platform scales the shop.
      #
      # Rendered into a HorizontalPodAutoscaler, so `replicas` above is only where the
      # deployment starts: the controller decides the count from there, between the
      # floor and the ceiling here, aiming to keep each replica at the CPU target.
      #
      # `scaleDownStabilizationSeconds` is how far back the controller looks before it
      # believes a fall in load is real. Kubernetes defaults it to 300 {S2.3} - five minutes
      # of the highest recommendation it saw - because a controller acting on the
      # reading in front of it acts on a reading its own last action produced.
      autoscaling:
        minReplicas: 3 {S2.4}
        maxReplicas: 6 {S2.5}
        targetCpuPercent: 70 {S2.6}
        scaleDownStabilizationSeconds: 0 {S2.7}
      
      # The ports the shop serves on, each selected by name rather than number.
      #
      # Every port is named for the protocol it carries, then what it is for:
      # `<protocol>[-<purpose>]`. The platform's convention, applied estate-wide.
      ports:
        web:
          port: 8000 {S2.8}
          portName: http
        admin:
          port: 8081 {S2.9}
          portName: http-admin
        metrics:
          port: 9090 {S2.10}
          portName: http-metrics
      
      # Where the rendered-summary cache lives.
      #
      # The account page reads this cache before it works a shopper's spend figure
      # out, and recomputes when the cache has nothing or cannot be reached. So the
      # shop stays correct whatever is written here - it only stays *fast* while the
      # address is right.
      cache:
        host: cache.io-shop.svc.cluster.local
        port: 6380 {S2.11}

PR #535 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.
The document already states what set it off, in a section of its own: the change [P2] - suspected, not confirmed.

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: The deployment renamed the metrics port from `metrics` to `http-metrics` in deploy/values-production.yaml, but deploy/scrape.yaml at that revision still picks the endpoint to scrape by the name `metrics`. The ServiceMonitor selects by port name, and a name that matches no port does not raise an error to the operator. It just gives an empty target list, so Prometheus had nothing to scrape.
cause_in_plain_words: A planned renaming of the shop's network ports to a platform-wide naming rule also renamed the port the monitoring system collects the shop's measurements from, and the monitoring setup, which finds that port by its name, was not changed to match, so it had nothing to collect.
still_at_risk: Until a deploy carries a matching scrape port name, io-shop's metrics stay uncollected, and any real fault in the shop could go unseen by alerts that work from those metrics.
symptom: Shoppers saw nothing wrong, but the shop's metrics stopped arriving
causal_chain 1: Nobody using the shop was seen to have anything go wrong. What was seen instead: the shop's metrics stopped arriving, and the series went absent rather than crossing a threshold. (cites AL1; T5, under "What Argus did, in order"; G46bc, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; Gbac1, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 2: The metrics stopped because Prometheus had no target to scrape. At the revision that was running, the ServiceMonitor picks the endpoint by the port name `metrics` (S1), and no port at that revision has that name: the metrics port is named `http-metrics` (S2). The scrape config itself says that a name matching no port gives an empty target list, not an error. (cites S1, under "What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired"; S2, under "What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired")
causal_chain 3: No port was named `metrics` any more because the deploy of revision c3c36da at {P2.1} renamed every port to the `<protocol>[-<purpose>]` convention, including the metrics port, from `metrics` to `http-metrics` (D1). As of {T13.1}, all replicas were running that revision. (cites P2, under "Changes to production it read"; D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed"; T13, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 3 ruled_out 1: The earlier deploy of revision 2c8f731: metrics were still collected with it in place, up to the minute before the onset. (cites P1, under "Changes to production it read"; T5, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 4: The rename broke scraping because the change edited only deploy/values-production.yaml and left the scrape config still selecting the port by its old name. (cites D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed"; S1, under "What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired")
contributing_factors 1: No check was seen that the port name the ServiceMonitor selects agrees with the metrics port name in values-production.yaml. The scrape config at the revision that ran says that nothing checks this, so a change to only one of the two files could ship.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: A check that failed on the mismatch would have stopped the rename from going out without a matching change to the scrape config, so the metrics would not have stopped.
contributing_factors 2: When the ServiceMonitor selects a port name that matches no port, the operator does not raise an error; it gives an empty target list. No alert on an empty scrape target list was seen, so the gap was found only by the MetricsAbsent rule once samples had been missing for its window.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: An alert or error on a ServiceMonitor with no targets would have caught the mismatch as soon as the rollout finished, without waiting for the metrics to be absent for the whole window.
contributing_factors 3: The MetricsAbsent alert on io-shop paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.
contributing_factors 3 had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have been told directly and could have taken up the open fix and its deploy sooner, shortening the time the shop ran unwatched.
action_items 1: Make the check that the ServiceMonitor's endpoint port name matches the metrics port name in values-production.yaml a required CI gate on every change to deploy/, so a rename that updates only one file is blocked.
action_items 2: Add an alert that fires when the io-shop ServiceMonitor resolves to no scrape targets.
action_items 3: Route the MetricsAbsent alert on io-shop to the on-call rotation so it pages a person.
action_items 4: Once the scrape port fix is merged, deploy a revision that carries it to io-shop.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {T5.1} or {duration}, are figures code writes in from the row they name. They are not judged.
  - Action items propose what to do; they make no claim about the record.
  - Whether something went well, went wrong or was lucky is a judgement. Only a fact it states is judged.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
